Can a model tell when a risk is worth taking?

And when does playing safe cost more?

Models play backgammon, and an engine scores every move they make. We measure whether each risk a model takes is the right one, and what that costs. Every decision is public.

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

The same at the 0.02 margin (robustness)

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions

Hit risk only: being hit. Gammon risk and priming are not in it.

Setups met different positions; risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were. Paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

Big risks found: stake above 0.08. Big needless risks: the chosen play lost more than 0.08.

‡ Risks with a probability: decisions whose plays were split into groups have no single probability and are left out; their count is shown per row. Setups that return no probabilities show N/A. Confidence on the call: ranking score only, no calibration gap (the probability is for the chosen play, not the risk). Definitions

Ability, caution and the SDT reference: A simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. The cost-derived SDT reference uses the setup's own mean equity lost per needless and per missed risk; those costs depend on the setup's own play, so it is a reference under that model, not the best caution, and a correctly classified call can still lose equity. Rates corrected by adding 0.5 to the counts and 1 to the totals; a setup without Risk pays or Safety pays decisions shows N/A. Intervals: 95%, blocks of two seat-swapped games resampled. Definitions
